Skip the failure part and immediately jump to the lesson, minimising the difficulty of what happened.

levels.title: Giving Honest Feedback to a Friend

levels.title: Asking Your Manager for Clarification

Ask a colleague what they think your manager meant, rather than going back to the source.

levels.title: Sending a Professional Email

levels.title: Making a Follow-Up Call

mcq.correct_feedback: Great call! A brief context reminder, a curious question about their review, and an invitation to discuss — that's professional and pressure-free.

levels.title: Giving a Status Update

Only mention the tasks that are going well to maintain a positive impression.
Tell them you're working on everything and will send a more detailed email later.

levels.title: Requesting Feedback on Your Work

Send a long email asking for written feedback with a list of specific questions to answer.

levels.title: Flagging a Task Is Taking Longer Than Expected

Wait until the end of the day to see if you can finish it before raising the issue.
Ask a colleague to cover for you so that the deadline appears to have been met.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right — proactive, early communication with context and a plan shows ownership and gives your manager time to adjust.

levels.title: Clearing Up a Misunderstanding
levels.scenario: A colleague has been cold with you for two days. You discover it's because they misheard something you said about them in a conversation last week.

mcq.question: What is the best way to address this misunderstanding?
mcq.correct_option: Approach them privately, acknowledge that you've sensed a shift, explain gently what you actually said versus what may have been heard, and invite them to share their perspective.
incorrect_options: Send them a message saying 'I think there's been a misunderstanding' without any further context.
Wait for them to come to you because you feel you shouldn't have to defend what you didn't say.
Address it in front of others so there is a witness to your clarification.
mcq.correct_feedback: Well done. A private, direct, empathetic conversation is the fastest and most respectful way to clear the air.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach is too vague, too passive, or too public. Misunderstandings clear best in private, direct, human conversation. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to approach your colleague and clear up the misunderstanding between you.
response.success_feedback: That conversation took courage and class. You addressed it directly, gave them full context, and made space for their perspective. The air is clear now.

levels.title: Standing Firm Under Group Pressure
levels.scenario: In a meeting, you made a recommendation based on solid research. A senior colleague disagrees loudly and others in the room seem to be swaying toward their view.

mcq.question: How do you hold your position under group and social pressure?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the dissenting view with respect, restate your reasoning calmly and clearly, and reference the evidence behind your recommendation.
incorrect_options: Back down and agree with the senior colleague to avoid prolonging the disagreement in front of others.
Repeat your original point louder and more emphatically to re-establish your position.
Ask the group to vote on it immediately to resolve the dispute without more discussion.
mcq.correct_feedback: Strong! Respectful acknowledgment plus clear evidence is how confident professionals hold their ground without becoming combative.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either surrenders good thinking, escalates, or bypasses proper discussion. Calm, evidence-backed persistence is the right move. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to restate and defend your recommendation in front of the group after being challenged.
response.success_feedback: Excellent! You held your ground with composure and evidence. That's the kind of confidence that earns long-term respect, even from those who disagreed.

levels.title: Preventing Escalation
levels.scenario: A conversation with a colleague about project ownership is getting increasingly tense and starting to feel personal. Voices are slightly raised.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to de-escalate before it becomes a full argument?
mcq.correct_option: Lower your own voice, pause the content of the debate, acknowledge that you both care about this, and suggest stepping away briefly or continuing in a calmer format.
incorrect_options: Make your point more forcefully one more time to get the last word in before backing down.
Walk away from the conversation abruptly to cool off without explaining yourself.
Call in your manager to mediate immediately so neither of you has to continue the discussion.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Lowering your energy first, naming the tension, and offering a reset is how skilled communicators defuse without surrendering.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either escalates, abandons without resolution, or escalates to a third party prematurely. Control your own energy first. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to de-escalate this tense conversation with your colleague before it becomes a real argument.
response.success_feedback: Well de-escalated! You brought the temperature down without backing away from the issue. That kind of emotional regulation is a rare and valuable skill.

levels.title: Respectfully Challenging Your Manager
levels.scenario: Your manager has made a decision about your team's workflow that you believe will slow everyone down and reduce quality. You want to raise it.

mcq.question: What is the most professional way to push back on your manager's decision?
mcq.correct_option: Ask for a private moment, acknowledge their reasoning, then present your concern with specific evidence and propose an alternative approach for their consideration.
incorrect_options: Raise your concerns in the team meeting so others can support your position.
Comply with the decision but communicate your frustration to your colleagues instead.
Send a long email detailing all the ways the decision is likely to go wrong.
mcq.correct_feedback: Perfectly handled. Private, respectful, evidence-led pushback with an alternative shows professional maturity and genuine care for the outcome.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either undermines your manager publicly, builds passive resistance, or escalates without dialogue. A direct, private, professional conversation is the right first step. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to raise your concern about your manager's decision in a private, respectful conversation.
response.success_feedback: Really well navigated. You gave them your honest perspective with evidence and an alternative — that's how you influence upward without threatening the relationship.

levels.title: Mediating Between Colleagues
levels.scenario: Two colleagues on your team are in an ongoing conflict that is affecting team morale. Both have approached you separately to vent about the other.

mcq.question: What is the right approach when asked to mediate informally?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge each person's feelings individually, avoid taking sides, and offer to facilitate a joint conversation where both parties can speak and be heard.
incorrect_options: Listen to both sides separately and then tell each person what the other said about them.
Take the side of the person you believe is more in the right and encourage them to confront the other.
Tell both of them to sort it out themselves since it's not your responsibility.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly the right approach! Acknowledging each person without bias and creating a structured space for dialogue is real mediation.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either betrays confidence, reinforces division, or abandons people who need support. Neutral facilitation is the most helpful and professional response. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to explain to one of the colleagues how you'd like to help mediate the situation.
response.success_feedback: That was measured and wise. You stepped in as a neutral bridge, not a judge — and that's exactly what good informal mediation looks like.

levels.title: Voicing Dissent in a Group Decision
levels.scenario: Your team has just agreed on a plan. You realise the plan has a significant risk you don't think was fully addressed.

mcq.question: What is the best way to raise your concern without derailing the decision?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge that the group has reached a decision, note that you support the direction overall, and then specifically name the risk you see and ask if it has been considered.
incorrect_options: Announce that you cannot support the decision until your concern has been fully resolved.
Say nothing in the meeting but flag the risk to your manager privately after the fact.
Start the conversation by apologising for not being more engaged earlier before making your point.
mcq.correct_feedback: Well played! Supporting the direction while naming a specific risk is constructive dissent — it adds value without derailing momentum.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either blocks progress unnecessarily, bypasses the group, or leads with an apology that undermines your point. Specific and constructive is the goal. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to raise your concern about the risk in this group decision in a constructive way.
response.success_feedback: Really smart contribution. You supported the group while adding important value. That's how you dissent in a way that makes the team stronger.

levels.title: Responding to Unfair Criticism
levels.scenario: In a team debrief, a senior leader criticises the quality of a piece of work — but they are wrong about the facts, and the work was actually strong.

mcq.question: What is the best way to respond to criticism you believe is unfair or factually incorrect?
mcq.correct_option: Stay composed, thank them for the feedback, and then calmly correct the record with specific facts — without becoming defensive or dismissive of their concern.
incorrect_options: Stay silent and accept the criticism publicly, then address it in a private email later.
Challenge them immediately and confidently to show the room that you know your work.
Ask a colleague who knows the facts to speak up on your behalf instead.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent. Staying calm while correcting the record with facts — respectfully — is both confident and professional.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either concedes wrongly, becomes confrontational, or deflects your own accountability. Calm, factual, self-assured is the right combination. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respectfully correct the factual error in the senior leader's criticism of your work.
response.success_feedback: That was composed and well-executed. You stood up for accurate information without ego, and that earns respect from even the most critical audience.

levels.title: Finding Compromise
levels.scenario: You and a colleague both want to lead an important upcoming project. Your manager has asked both of you to come back with a joint proposal.

mcq.question: What is the best approach to finding a workable compromise?
mcq.correct_option: Start the conversation by each naming what is most important to you about leading the project, then look for a structure where each person's core needs are met.
incorrect_options: Propose splitting the project evenly down the middle as a fair starting point.
Make the case for why you should lead and hope they concede once they see your reasoning.
Let your colleague take the lead role since you don't want to cause tension over it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Understanding each other's underlying interests — not just positions — is the foundation of genuine compromise.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either forces an arbitrary split, becomes a one-sided argument, or surrenders too easily. Real compromise starts with understanding what matters to each side. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open the compromise conversation with your colleague and begin working toward a joint proposal.
response.success_feedback: Beautifully opened! You started with interests rather than positions — that creates the conditions for a real and lasting solution you both feel good about.

levels.title: Making a Strong First Impression
levels.scenario: You are walking into a final round job interview with a panel of three senior professionals. This is your best opportunity at a role you really want.

mcq.question: Which behaviour best sets the tone for a strong first impression?
mcq.correct_option: Enter confidently, make eye contact with each panellist, offer a firm handshake, use each person's name when introduced, and sit with engaged posture.

Start with a self-deprecating comment to put the panel at ease and show humility.
Wait until the formal Q&A begins before making any real impression — the greeting is just formality.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent! Eye contact, names, posture, and a confident entry communicate competence before you say a single word about your experience.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either misses the opportunity, undermines your credibility immediately, or treats the greeting as insignificant — it isn't. First impressions begin in the first 10 seconds. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to walk into this panel interview room and make your opening impression count.

levels.title: Speaking Up in a Large Meeting
levels.scenario: You are in a company-wide meeting with senior stakeholders. There is a relevant point you want to make, but you have been hesitating for several minutes.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to enter a large, senior meeting with a contribution?
mcq.correct_option: Wait for a natural gap, signal your intent with 'I'd like to add something here if I may,' then make your point clearly and concisely in two or three sentences.

Talk over the current speaker slightly to ensure you get your point in before the topic moves on.
Write your point in the meeting notes document and hope someone reads it aloud.
mcq.correct_feedback: Perfectly executed. A brief signal, a clear contribution, and a concise delivery shows confidence without arrogance.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach is either too passive, disruptive, or invisible. In a senior setting, your voice needs to be heard — directly and purposefully. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to make your contribution in this large senior meeting confidently and clearly.
response.success_feedback: Well done for speaking up! Your contribution was clear, confident, and well-timed. That's how you build visibility and credibility in senior environments.

levels.title: Networking at a Professional Event
levels.scenario: You are at a formal industry conference where you don't know anyone. You want to make two or three meaningful professional connections.

mcq.question: What is the most effective networking approach at an event like this?
mcq.correct_option: Approach people who are standing alone or on the edge of groups, introduce yourself briefly, ask a genuine question about their work, and focus on quality of conversation over quantity of contacts.
incorrect_options: Collect as many business cards as possible by working the room at speed.
Wait near the refreshments and let conversations happen organically without initiating.
Spend most of your time with people from your own company since you already know them.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Targeting approachable people, asking real questions, and going for depth over breadth leads to connections that actually last.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either stays surface-level, too passive, or defeats the whole purpose of attending. Meaningful connections come from genuine conversation. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to approach someone you don't know at this conference and start a genuine professional conversation.
response.success_feedback: Great networking! You led with real curiosity and created the foundation for an actual professional relationship — not just an exchanged business card.

levels.title: Asking for a Promotion
levels.scenario: You have been in your current role for 18 months, consistently exceed your targets, and have taken on responsibilities beyond your job description. Your review is tomorrow.

mcq.question: What is the most effective approach to having this conversation with your manager?
mcq.correct_option: Request a specific meeting for this purpose, come prepared with a summary of your achievements and the additional responsibilities you've taken on, and state clearly that you would like to discuss next steps for your career.
incorrect_options: Bring up the promotion at the end of your regular check-in when a few minutes are left.
Tell your manager you've been approached by another company to create urgency.
Ask for a promotion by saying you feel you deserve one without providing specific evidence.
mcq.correct_feedback: Very well prepared! A dedicated meeting, concrete evidence, and a clear ask shows you're ready for the next level — in substance and in approach.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either gives the topic too little space, creates artificial pressure, or lacks the evidence to support the ask. A strong case needs preparation and a proper stage. Try again!

levels.title: Managing Up Effectively
levels.scenario: Your manager is known for making fast decisions without always considering the team's input. A new decision affecting your work was made without consultation.

mcq.question: How do you proactively shape your manager's decision-making process without overstepping?
mcq.correct_option: Request a brief regular check-in where you can share ground-level perspectives before decisions are made, and frame it as a way to give them better information.
incorrect_options: Escalate the issue to your manager's manager to show that decisions need to involve the team.
Complain to colleagues about the lack of consultation to build shared frustration.
Simply adapt to the decision without raising the issue since it's your manager's prerogative.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really smart! Proposing a structure that gives your manager better input — framed in their interest — is the most effective form of managing up.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either escalates prematurely, builds resentment without resolution, or enables a pattern that will continue. Influence upward through value and structure. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to have the conversation with your manager about improving how decisions are made together.
response.success_feedback: Excellent! You proposed a process improvement in a way that served everyone — including your manager. That kind of upward influence is what distinguishes great professionals.

levels.title: Saying No to Extra Work
levels.scenario: Your manager asks you to take on an additional project. You are already at full capacity and taking this on would compromise the quality of your existing work.

mcq.question: How do you say no professionally without damaging your standing?
mcq.correct_option: Be transparent about your current workload, explain what would be at risk if you took this on, and offer to discuss what could be deprioritised to make room — putting the choice back to your manager.
incorrect_options: Say yes and find a way to manage, even if it means working evenings and weekends.
Decline with a vague 'I'm pretty busy right now' without explaining the actual capacity conflict.
Tell your manager you'll take it on if they can find something to take off your plate, as a trade.
mcq.correct_feedback: Very well handled! Transparency about capacity, risk of existing work, and a collaborative path forward puts the decision in the right hands — your manager's.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either burns you out, lacks specifics, or frames it as a transaction. A professional no is honest, specific, and forward-looking. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to tell your manager you cannot take on this additional project — professionally and with full transparency.
response.success_feedback: Handled with real professionalism! You were honest, responsible, and solution-focused. Your manager now has the information they need to make a good decision.

levels.title: Communicating Across Departments
levels.scenario: You need a piece of work from a colleague in another department to move your project forward. They are not your direct colleague and the request is time-sensitive.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to make this cross-departmental request?
mcq.correct_option: Reach out directly, briefly explain the context and why their input matters to the wider project, specify exactly what you need, and be upfront about the timeline.
incorrect_options: Ask your manager to make the request on your behalf so it carries more authority.
Send a vague 'when you get a chance' request without mentioning urgency.
CC their manager on the request from the start to ensure accountability.
mcq.correct_feedback: Well done! Direct, context-rich, specific, and honest about urgency — that's how you get timely help from people who have no formal obligation to you.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either delays things, obscures urgency, or creates unnecessary political dynamics from the start. A clear, direct, respectful ask works best. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to reach out to this colleague in another department and make your time-sensitive request.
response.success_feedback: Clear, considerate, and effective! You gave them everything they needed to say yes quickly — context, specifics, and honest timing. That's how cross-functional relationships are built.

levels.title: Writing a Clear Workplace Message
levels.scenario: You need to send a message to your whole team about a process change that will affect how they submit their weekly reports starting next Monday.

mcq.question: What makes this kind of team communication most effective?
mcq.correct_option: State the change at the top, explain briefly why it is happening, specify the exact new steps they need to follow, and state the effective date clearly.
incorrect_options: Provide extensive background on the reason for the change before explaining what they need to do.
Tell them a change is coming and that you'll send more details in a follow-up message.
Send a casual message asking them to 'keep an eye out for a new process' without specifics.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent! Leading with the change, giving concise context, clear steps, and a date removes all ambiguity — which is what makes team communication effective.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach buries the main point, delays the information people need, or leaves too much vague. Clarity first, context second. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to draft the core message you would send to your team about this process change.
response.success_feedback: Perfectly structured! You led with the change, explained the why, gave clear steps, and specified the start date. That message will be understood and acted on — which is the whole point.

levels.title: Addressing an Uncomfortable Workplace Situation
levels.scenario: A colleague made a comment in a team meeting that you found inappropriate and exclusionary, though others didn't call it out at the time.

mcq.question: What is the most professional way to address this?
mcq.correct_option: Speak to the colleague privately after the meeting, describe what was said, explain specifically why it felt inappropriate, and give them the chance to respond.
incorrect_options: Report it directly to HR without speaking to the colleague first, to create an official record.
Mention it in the next team meeting as an example of the kind of thing that shouldn't happen.
Let it go this time but keep a mental note to monitor whether it happens again.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! A private, direct, specific conversation is almost always the right first step. It addresses the issue while giving the person a chance to understand and improve.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either escalates too fast, makes the issue public, or does nothing. A respectful private conversation is the first and usually most effective step. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address this colleague privately about the comment they made in the meeting.
response.success_feedback: Really courageous and professional. You named the specific issue, gave them context for why it mattered, and handled it directly — that takes real strength.

levels.title: Advocating for Your Team
levels.scenario: Leadership has announced a new initiative that will add significant workload to your already-stretched team without additional resources or timeline adjustments.

mcq.question: How do you advocate effectively for your team in this situation?
mcq.correct_option: Request time with the decision-maker, come prepared with specific data on current capacity, outline the realistic impact of the new initiative, and propose at least one solution.

Send a strongly worded group email to leadership expressing frustration on behalf of your team.
Agree to the initiative publicly but slow-roll the implementation so the team doesn't feel the pressure.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent advocacy! Evidence-based, solution-oriented pushback in a direct conversation with the right person is how a great leader protects their team.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either abandons your team, antagonises leadership, or is dishonest. Real advocacy means speaking up directly, with data, and with a path forward. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to make your case to the decision-maker on behalf of your team's capacity and wellbeing.
response.success_feedback: Really strong advocacy! You came prepared, stayed professional, and made the impact clear — while proposing solutions. That's leadership speaking truth to power.

levels.title: Getting Buy-In on a New Idea
levels.scenario: You have an idea that could significantly improve your team's workflow, but you need your colleagues to adopt a new process they haven't used before.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to get your colleagues on board with a new idea?
mcq.correct_option: Frame the idea around the problem it solves for them specifically, share early results or examples, and involve them in shaping how it gets implemented.
incorrect_options: Present all the details of your idea comprehensively and let them decide whether to adopt it.
Get your manager's endorsement first and then announce the change as a top-down decision.
Send an email with the full proposal and ask for feedback, expecting most people to respond.
mcq.correct_feedback: Brilliant! Problem-first framing, evidence, and co-ownership creates genuine buy-in — not just compliance.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either overwhelms, bypasses peer buy-in, or relies on a communication channel that rarely generates real engagement. People support what they help build. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to pitch your workflow improvement idea to a key colleague whose buy-in you need most.
response.success_feedback: Really persuasive! You made it about their problem, showed it works, and gave them a voice in the process. That's the formula for genuine adoption.

levels.title: Overcoming Objections
levels.scenario: You have proposed a new initiative and a colleague raises a strong objection that you believe is based on incomplete information.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to respond to a genuine objection to your proposal?
mcq.correct_option: Thank them for raising it, acknowledge it is a real concern, and then address it directly with specific information they may not have had — asking if that changes anything for them.
incorrect_options: Dismiss the objection quickly to stay on track and prevent others from piling on.
Ask why they feel that way repeatedly until they run out of objections.
Concede the point and modify the entire proposal on the spot to accommodate their concern.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent! Validating the objection before addressing it signals confidence, not weakness — and asking if it changes things invites real dialogue.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either dismisses, pressure-tests, or over-concedes. A well-handled objection is an opportunity to strengthen your case. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this objection in a way that is confident, respectful, and persuasive.
response.success_feedback: Well handled! You didn't flinch at the pushback — you welcomed it, addressed it with facts, and kept the conversation productive. That's persuasion at its best.

levels.title: Pitching Under Time Pressure

mcq.question: What should you prioritise in a pitch when time is extremely limited?

Spend the first minute building rapport and context before getting to the actual proposal.
Rush through as much of the prepared pitch as possible and hand out the full deck afterward.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Problem, solution, evidence, ask. In three minutes, every word must earn its place.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either overloads, delays the point, or turns the pitch into a race. In a tight window, the structure that matters most is: problem — solution — evidence — ask. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver your 3-minute pitch to the leadership team with maximum impact.
response.success_feedback: Incredibly sharp! You got to the point fast, gave them what they needed to say yes, and respected everyone's time. That is how ideas get funded in the real world.

levels.title: Convincing a Sceptical Stakeholder
levels.scenario: A senior stakeholder is resistant to a change you are proposing. They haven't said no outright, but they keep deferring and raising concerns.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to move a sceptical stakeholder toward a decision?
mcq.correct_option: Ask what specific concern or missing information is preventing them from committing, then address that specific issue directly and concisely.
incorrect_options: Present the full business case again with more detail, hoping more information will tip them.
Give them a deadline to decide and make clear the window for approval is closing.
Get others in their network to advocate for the idea so the stakeholder sees wider support.
mcq.correct_feedback: Spot on! Diagnosing the actual blocker is far more effective than more data or external pressure. Ask, then address.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either overwhelms, pressures, or bypasses the real issue. The fastest path through scepticism is understanding exactly what is causing it. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to have the conversation that moves this sceptical stakeholder off the fence.
response.success_feedback: Very well navigated! You found the real sticking point and addressed it directly. That's how you turn 'maybe' into 'yes' — one specific concern at a time.

levels.title: Using Storytelling to Persuade
levels.scenario: You are trying to convince your leadership team to invest in a new employee wellbeing programme. The data supports it, but the room seems unmoved.

mcq.question: What communication approach would most effectively complement the data you have already shared?
mcq.correct_option: Tell a brief, specific story about a real (anonymised) team member whose experience illustrates exactly why this programme matters — making the data human.

Tell them how much you personally believe in this programme and why it means a lot to you.
Reference what competitor companies are doing so leadership doesn't want to fall behind.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! A real story that puts a face to the data is far more persuasive than more data. People feel stories in a way they can't feel numbers.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either piles on data that already isn't landing, makes it personal in a way that doesn't scale, or relies on fear. A human story changes everything. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the human story that will bring your wellbeing programme proposal to life.
response.success_feedback: Powerfully done. You took something that was just numbers and made it real. That story will stay with people long after the meeting — and that's what drives decisions.

levels.title: Getting Agreement on a Change

mcq.question: How do you bring resistant people along on a change they haven't chosen?

Keep mentioning how other teams are already using it successfully to create positive peer pressure.
Let them continue using the old tool for now and hope they come around naturally over time.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really well thought through! Honesty about the cost, specificity about the benefit, support during transition, and a willing early adopter — that's change management done right.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either forces compliance without conviction, uses peer pressure, or allows indefinite resistance. Real adoption requires empathy and a strong why. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to persuade your most resistant colleague to give the new tool a genuine try.
response.success_feedback: Beautifully persuasive! You were honest about the effort required and specific about the reward. That combination of realism and optimism is what moves people.

levels.title: Recommending a Different Approach

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to recommend a change to a manager who prefers the status quo?

Ask your manager directly why they haven't tried other approaches and whether they'd be open to it.
Share an article about the approach and forward it without context, hoping they'll draw their own conclusions.
mcq.correct_feedback: Brilliant! Results from a real trial are far more persuasive than any proposal. You proved it before asking for buy-in.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either implies the current way is wrong (which creates defensiveness), puts them on the spot, or is too indirect. Evidence from a real test is the most credible argument. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to share your trial results and recommend the new approach to your manager.
response.success_feedback: Very smart persuasion. You did the work before making the ask — and that made your recommendation virtually unanswerable. That's influence with evidence.

levels.title: Influencing Without Authority
levels.scenario: You are a peer, not a manager, but you need a colleague to change how they are approaching a shared piece of work — their current method is creating problems for you.

mcq.question: How do you effectively influence a colleague when you have no authority over them?
mcq.correct_option: Explain specifically how their current approach is creating a downstream problem for you, connect it to the shared goal you both care about, and propose a practical change — framing it as a collaboration.
incorrect_options: Ask your manager to have a word with them about the issue on your behalf.
Adapt your own workflow to absorb the impact of their approach rather than raise the issue.
Tell them you'd prefer they worked differently, without explaining the specific impact on you.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Impact, shared goal, collaborative solution — that's the framework for peer influence that actually works.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either escalates unnecessarily, avoids the issue, or lacks the specificity that turns a vague request into real action. Direct peer persuasion with a clear why wins. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to have the conversation with this colleague about changing how you are both working together.
response.success_feedback: Really effective! You named the impact, connected it to the shared goal, and proposed a solution — without making it personal. That's peer leadership at its best.

levels.title: Making a Case for Resources
levels.scenario: Your team is understaffed and it is affecting output quality. You want to request an additional headcount in your next conversation with your director.

mcq.question: How do you make the strongest case for additional resources?
mcq.correct_option: Present a clear picture of current workload versus capacity, quantify the business impact of the gap, and calculate the return on investment of the additional headcount.
incorrect_options: Tell your director that the team is exhausted and morale is low to appeal to their empathy.
Say that you've been requesting this for a while and something needs to happen soon.
Compare your team size to other teams in the organisation to show you are understaffed relative to them.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent! Workload data plus business impact plus ROI is the language of resource decisions. You made the business case, not just the emotional one.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach appeals to feelings, history, or relative comparison — none of which address the business logic a director needs. Numbers and impact win resource conversations. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to make your case for additional headcount to your director with data and clear impact.
response.success_feedback: That was a board-level argument in a manager's meeting. You backed the request with numbers, linked it to business outcomes, and made the ROI clear. Very impressive.

levels.title: Motivating Someone to Act
levels.scenario: A talented friend has been talking about starting their side project for six months but keeps putting it off. They mention it again over coffee.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to motivate them to take real action this time?
mcq.correct_option: Ask them what specifically is stopping them, address the real obstacle with them, and help them identify one concrete first step they can take this week.
incorrect_options: Give an inspiring speech about how life is short and they should just go for it.
Tell them how disappointed you'd be if they don't follow through on this dream.
Share a success story of someone else who started a business to inspire them by comparison.
mcq.correct_feedback: Perfect! Diagnosing the real blocker and anchoring to a specific first step is far more effective than inspiration alone.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either motivates in the moment without changing the pattern, uses guilt, or makes it about someone else's story. Real motivation comes from removing the real obstacle. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to help your friend identify what is actually stopping them and commit to a first concrete step.
response.success_feedback: That was genuinely helpful! You got past the surface-level encouragement and found the real blocker — and then you helped them move it. That's what true support looks like.

levels.title: Rallying a Discouraged Team
levels.scenario: Your team has just experienced a significant setback — a project they worked hard on was cancelled. Morale is visibly low.

mcq.question: What is the most effective first thing to say to your team after a demoralising setback?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the disappointment directly and genuinely, thank them for the effort they put in, and then — when the moment is right — focus on what comes next.
incorrect_options: Immediately pivot to the next project to keep momentum and avoid dwelling on the setback.
Tell them not to be too disappointed since these things happen in business and it wasn't a big deal.
Focus on what the team could have done better so you can learn from it before moving forward.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. Before you can move people forward, you have to stand with them in the moment. Acknowledging the loss first is the foundation for what comes next.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either bypasses real feelings, minimises them, or adds criticism at the wrong moment. When a team is hurting, they need to be heard before they can be led. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address your team following this setback in a way that acknowledges how they feel and begins to restore energy.
response.success_feedback: That was real leadership. You let them feel what they needed to feel, honoured their work, and started building the bridge forward. That's how great leaders hold teams together in hard moments.

levels.title: Delivering Constructive Feedback
levels.scenario: A team member submitted a client-facing document with several significant errors that you had to catch and fix before it went out. This is the third time.

mcq.question: How do you deliver this feedback in a way that is direct, fair, and leads to change?
mcq.correct_option: Describe the specific pattern — not just the latest incident — explain the impact on the client and on you, and ask them what support or change would help prevent it going forward.
incorrect_options: Point out the errors in this specific document and ask them to be more careful next time.
Praise their other work first at length before mentioning the errors to soften the blow.
Tell them you're worried about their performance and ask if everything is okay personally.
mcq.correct_feedback: Well done! Naming the pattern (not just the incident), linking it to impact, and asking for their input on solutions creates real change — not just a temporary fix.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either addresses only the surface, buries the feedback, or conflates professional performance with personal circumstances. Specific, impact-focused, solution-oriented feedback works best. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver this pattern-focused, impact-centred feedback to your team member.
response.success_feedback: Really strong feedback delivery. You named the pattern, explained the impact, and turned it into a dialogue about solutions. That's how feedback actually changes behaviour.

levels.title: Setting Expectations with a New Hire
levels.scenario: A new team member has joined this week. You want to set clear expectations about how the team works without overwhelming them on day one.

mcq.question: What is the most effective approach to setting expectations with a new hire?
mcq.correct_option: Cover the three or four non-negotiable expectations in your first meeting, explain the reasoning behind each, and invite questions — spreading the rest across their first two weeks.
incorrect_options: Send them a detailed onboarding document covering all team standards and ask them to review it.
Let them settle in for a few weeks and observe how things work before setting formal expectations.
Set all expectations in one long meeting on day one so they are clear from the very beginning.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really well considered! Key expectations with rationale, in manageable doses, invites trust — not overwhelm.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either relies on a document rather than a conversation, leaves expectations vague too long, or dumps too much at once. Clear, staged, and conversational works best. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to share your key team expectations with the new hire in your first meeting together.
response.success_feedback: Excellent onboarding! You were clear about what matters most, explained the why, and made it feel like a conversation rather than a briefing. That new person will feel set up, not overwhelmed.

levels.title: Recognising a Team Member Publicly
levels.scenario: One of your team members went significantly above and beyond on a recent project that made a real difference to the client outcome.

mcq.question: What makes public recognition most meaningful and impactful?
mcq.correct_option: Name them specifically, describe the exact thing they did and why it was difficult, explain the impact it had, and deliver it in front of the relevant people — not just the whole company newsletter.
incorrect_options: Give them a general shout-out at the next all-hands meeting without going into specifics.
Send them a private message thanking them so they don't feel put on the spot.
Mention the project's success in a team email but attribute it to the whole team to avoid singling anyone out.
mcq.correct_feedback: Spot on! Specific, impact-linked recognition delivered in the right room is the most powerful form of professional appreciation.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either stays too vague, removes the public dimension, or dissolves the individual recognition into the team. The most meaningful recognition is specific, personal, and witnessed. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to publicly recognise your team member's contribution in front of the relevant people.
response.success_feedback: Beautiful recognition! You named them, described the specific thing they did, and linked it to real impact. That person will feel truly seen — and it will inspire the whole team.

levels.title: Delegating Effectively
levels.scenario: You need to delegate a high-stakes piece of work to a team member who has the skills but has not handled anything of this scale before.

mcq.question: What does an effective delegation conversation include?
mcq.correct_option: Explain the full context and why they were chosen, clarify the outcome expected rather than the exact method, agree on check-in points, and make clear they can come to you with questions.
incorrect_options: Give them the task with a deadline and trust them to figure out the details independently.
Walk them through every step of how to do the task so they are fully prepared.
Delegate the task but keep checking in daily to ensure quality and catch any issues early.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Context, outcome focus, agreed checkpoints, and an open door creates empowerment with appropriate support — that's effective delegation.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either under-prepares, over-directs, or micromanages. Great delegation sets someone up to succeed and then trusts them — with structure. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to delegate this high-stakes task to your team member in a way that sets them up to succeed.
response.success_feedback: Really well delegated! You gave them purpose, clarity, support, and space. That's how you develop people while getting things done — the hallmark of great leadership.

levels.title: Communicating Team Goals
levels.scenario: Leadership has set your team a challenging new set of targets for the quarter. You need to communicate these to the team in a way that creates ownership rather than resistance.

mcq.question: How do you communicate ambitious goals in a way that motivates rather than demoralises?
mcq.correct_option: Share the goals with full transparency, explain the strategic context behind them, acknowledge they are a stretch, and invite the team to identify what they need to achieve them.
incorrect_options: Present the goals confidently without acknowledging any difficulty so the team stays positive.
Tell the team these are leadership's targets, not yours, to manage their frustration.
Break the goals into individual targets and assign them without team discussion to avoid debate.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really smart! Transparency, context, honesty about the stretch, and involving the team in planning creates real ownership and belief.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either over-optimises, distances you from accountability, or removes the team's voice entirely. Owned goals are achieved; assigned goals are resented. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to communicate the new quarterly targets to your team in a way that inspires ownership.
response.success_feedback: Excellent! You were honest, gave context, and made the team part of the solution. That's the kind of goal communication that creates a team that runs toward a challenge — not away from it.

levels.title: Running an Effective Meeting
levels.scenario: You are about to facilitate a 45-minute team meeting on a complex topic. Previous meetings on this subject have run over and ended without clear decisions.

mcq.question: What is the most important thing to do to make this meeting actually productive?
mcq.correct_option: State the purpose and desired outcome at the start, time-box each agenda item, actively draw quieter voices into discussion, and close each point with an explicit decision or action before moving on.
incorrect_options: Send a detailed agenda in advance and trust that people will prepare and stick to it.
Keep the meeting informal and unstructured to encourage more creative conversation.
Let the most knowledgeable person in the room lead each topic to save time.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Purpose, time-boxing, inclusion, and explicit decisions at each stage is the blueprint for a meeting that actually achieves something.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either over-relies on preparation alone, loses focus, or creates a single-voice dynamic. The facilitator's job is active structure, not passive agenda management. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open this meeting in a way that sets it up to be focused, inclusive, and decisive.
response.success_feedback: Brilliant facilitation from the start! You set the purpose, named the outcome, and signalled how you'd run it. That first 60 seconds of a meeting determines everything that follows.

levels.title: Addressing a Performance Issue
levels.scenario: A team member has been missing deadlines and delivering below-standard work for five weeks. You have been hoping it would self-correct, but it hasn't.

mcq.question: What is the right approach at this stage?
mcq.correct_option: Have a direct private conversation, name the pattern you have observed over the past five weeks with specific examples, ask if there is something affecting their performance, and be clear about the standard expected.
incorrect_options: Wait a little longer to see if things improve before having what could be an uncomfortable conversation.
Give them increasingly difficult tasks to signal that their performance needs to improve.
Talk to the rest of the team to understand whether they've noticed the same issues before speaking to the person.
mcq.correct_feedback: Right call, and not a moment too soon. Naming the pattern, checking for context, and restating the standard is the compassionate and professional approach to a performance issue.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either delays a conversation that should have happened weeks ago, is passive-aggressive, or involves others before the person themselves. Direct, private, specific, and caring is the way. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open this performance conversation with your team member — directly, fairly, and with genuine care.
response.success_feedback: Really well done for having that conversation. You named the facts, asked the human question, and restated the standard. That's the kind of feedback conversation that can genuinely turn things around.

levels.title: Creating Psychological Safety
levels.scenario: You have noticed your team rarely challenges ideas, disagrees in meetings, or raises concerns — even when you invite them to. This is a pattern, not a one-off.

mcq.question: What is the most effective thing you can do as a leader to build psychological safety?
mcq.correct_option: Model it yourself — visibly share your own mistakes, welcome dissenting views when they arise, and follow through by acting on feedback the team gives you.
incorrect_options: Announce to the team that this is a safe space and encourage them to speak up more going forward.
Ask individual team members privately if they feel comfortable sharing their views.
Introduce a weekly anonymous feedback form so people can share concerns without risk.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Psychological safety is built through consistent leader behaviour — not announcements or tools. When you model vulnerability, you give the team permission to do the same.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes promises without proof, surfaces symptoms rather than causes, or creates a workaround instead of the real culture. Behaviour change starts with the leader. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to share with your team — in your own words — a time you were wrong and what you learned from it.
response.success_feedback: Powerfully done. By sharing your own vulnerability openly, you just gave every person in that room permission to be imperfect too. That's how psychological safety is actually built.

levels.title: Leading Through Uncertainty
levels.scenario: Your organisation is going through a major restructure. You don't have all the details yet, but your team is anxious and asking you questions you can't fully answer.

mcq.question: What is the right thing to say when your team needs reassurance but you don't have all the answers?
mcq.correct_option: Be honest that you don't have all the details yet, share what you do know, commit to passing information on as soon as you have it, and acknowledge that the uncertainty is difficult.
incorrect_options: Tell them everything will be fine and not to worry, to prevent panic spreading in the team.
Wait until you have full information before addressing the team, to avoid speculation.
Encourage them to focus on their work and not pay attention to what's happening at the organisation level.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Honest uncertainty, plus what you do know, plus a commitment to communicate, plus empathy — that's the formula for leading well when you don't have the map.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes promises you can't keep, leaves the team in silence, or dismisses legitimate concern. People can handle uncertainty — what they can't handle is being misled or ignored. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address your team's anxiety about the restructure with honesty and steadying confidence.
response.success_feedback: That was leadership at its most real. You didn't pretend, you didn't minimise, and you didn't disappear. You showed up honestly — and that is exactly what your team needed.

levels.title: Telling a Friend Something Hard
levels.scenario: You have noticed that a close friend's romantic partner treats them poorly in public, and your friend seems to be slowly changing for the worse. You are worried.

mcq.question: How do you raise this concern with your friend without damaging the friendship or pushing them away?
mcq.correct_option: Choose a private, calm moment, share what you've observed and how it has made you feel with specific examples, make clear you're saying this because you care, and then listen without pushing for an immediate response.
incorrect_options: Wait until they come to you with a problem about the relationship before raising your concerns.
Tell them directly that their partner is toxic and they should leave the relationship.
Raise the topic in front of other friends so they know they're not alone in feeling this way.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really well handled. Specific observations, leading with love, and then giving them space to process — that's how you plant a seed without creating a wall.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either waits too long, goes too far too fast, or makes the conversation public when it should be private. This conversation belongs between the two of you — gently and at the right moment. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to share your honest concern with your friend about what you've been observing.
response.success_feedback: That was a courageous act of friendship. You named what you saw, framed it with love, and gave them space. Not everyone has a friend willing to say the hard thing — yours does.

levels.title: Confronting Someone Who Takes Credit
levels.scenario: A colleague has presented ideas from your one-on-one conversations as their own in team meetings on two separate occasions.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to address this directly and professionally?
mcq.correct_option: Speak to them privately, reference the specific instances calmly, explain the impact this has on your professional reputation, and make clear what you expect going forward.
incorrect_options: Start contributing ideas only in writing so there is always a record you can point to.
Call them out in the next team meeting when it happens again so it stops immediately.
Mention it to your manager and let them handle the conversation on your behalf.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. Private, direct, specific, and clear about expectations — that's the most effective and professional route to resolving this.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either works around the problem, creates a public scene, or escalates before trying direct resolution. A private, direct conversation is always the right first step. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to confront this colleague privately about taking credit for your ideas.
response.success_feedback: Really well done for having that conversation. You named the specific incidents, explained the impact, and made the boundary clear — calmly and directly. That took real professionalism.

levels.title: Rebuilding Trust After It Has Been Broken
levels.scenario: You shared something in confidence with a colleague and found out they told others. You have to work closely with them and want to address it honestly.

mcq.question: What is the most constructive way to approach this conversation?
mcq.correct_option: Bring it up privately, name what happened clearly without accusing, say how it affected you, ask for their perspective, and explain what you would need from them going forward.
incorrect_options: Confront them in front of others to make the seriousness of the breach clear.
Decide you can no longer trust them and create professional distance without explanation.
Accept the apology quickly if they offer one and move on without naming what you need going forward.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really mature. Naming what happened, sharing the impact, hearing their side, and naming what you need going forward — that's how you give trust a chance to rebuild.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes it public, avoids it, or closes the loop before it's really been dealt with. Trust is rebuilt through honest, direct, private conversation. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address this breach of trust with your colleague in a way that is direct but opens a path forward.
response.success_feedback: That was handled with remarkable maturity. You were honest without being punishing, and you created the conditions for trust to potentially be rebuilt. That's hard to do.

levels.title: Bringing Up a Sensitive Personal Topic
levels.scenario: You are worried that a sibling's drinking has crossed from social to problematic. You have been putting off this conversation for months.

mcq.question: How do you approach this kind of deeply personal, sensitive topic with someone you love?
mcq.correct_option: Choose a calm, sober, private moment. Lead with love and concern — not diagnosis or judgment. Share specific things you have observed and ask open questions rather than making statements.
incorrect_options: Research alcohol dependency and present information and statistics to make your case clinically.
Bring it up when they have been drinking so that the behaviour is fresh in their mind.
Ask their partner or another family member to raise it on your behalf to reduce conflict.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. The right moment, the right tone, and specific observations with open questions — that's how you open a door that someone has the ability to walk through.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either turns love into a case study, chooses the worst possible moment, or removes your own voice from a conversation that should come from you. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open this difficult conversation with your sibling from a place of love and honest concern.
response.success_feedback: That took tremendous courage. You led with love, you shared what you've observed, and you asked rather than told. That's how you keep the door open in the hardest conversations.

levels.title: Addressing Inappropriate Remarks
levels.scenario: During a team lunch, a colleague made a joke that was offensive to a particular group of people. Others laughed uncomfortably. You want to say something.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to address this without creating a scene?
mcq.correct_option: Respond calmly in the moment with a brief, non-attacking observation such as 'I think that one didn't quite land for me' — and follow up privately with the colleague afterward if needed.
incorrect_options: Ignore it in the moment but report it to HR to create a formal record.
Immediately confront the person with a detailed explanation of why the joke was offensive in front of everyone.
Send them a message after the lunch explaining why what they said was problematic.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really well calibrated. A soft, non-attacking in-the-moment signal — followed by a private conversation if needed — is the most effective and proportionate response.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either over-escalates, creates a public confrontation, or leaves the remark entirely unchallenged in the room where it happened. A measured immediate response is most powerful. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this inappropriate remark — in the moment and in a way that is calm, clear, and effective.
response.success_feedback: Handled with real poise. You named it without attacking, which is far more likely to create actual reflection than a public confrontation. Well done for speaking up.

levels.title: Setting Boundaries
levels.scenario: A close friend keeps calling you for emotional support late at night and it is affecting your sleep and your own mental health. You need to set a boundary.

mcq.question: How do you set this boundary in a way that protects yourself without rejecting your friend?
mcq.correct_option: Tell them honestly that late-night calls are affecting you, express that you still want to be there for them, and propose a different time or format that works for both of you.
incorrect_options: Stop picking up the calls without explanation and hope they understand the message.
Tell them you're going through a lot yourself and don't have capacity for their issues right now.
Say you're happy to talk any time they need but then feel resentful when the calls continue.
mcq.correct_feedback: Perfectly balanced! Honest about the impact, clear about the boundary, and still showing care — that's a boundary conversation that strengthens rather than damages a relationship.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either avoids the conversation, creates distance without explanation, or sets no real boundary at all. A real boundary needs to be spoken clearly and kindly. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to set this boundary with your friend in a way that is loving, honest, and clear.
response.success_feedback: That was a really healthy conversation. You protected your own wellbeing while holding the friendship. Boundaries said with love are not walls — they're what makes relationships sustainable.

levels.title: Working Through a Major Disagreement
levels.scenario: You and your partner have a recurring argument about a major financial decision that neither of you feels heard on. The conversation always ends in frustration.

mcq.question: What communication approach is most likely to break the pattern and produce real resolution?
mcq.correct_option: Agree to set aside time specifically for this conversation, take turns speaking without interruption, and focus on understanding each other's underlying concern — not winning the argument.
incorrect_options: Make your case more thoroughly this time using data and logic to demonstrate your position is correct.
Wait for a moment when they seem in a particularly good mood and raise it then.
Agree to table the decision indefinitely to avoid another argument about it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really wise! Breaking the pattern requires a new structure — dedicated time, turn-taking, and a goal of understanding rather than winning.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either repeats what hasn't worked, adds mood-dependency to a serious topic, or avoids the issue entirely. New outcomes require new approaches. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open this conversation differently — in a way that finally makes space for both of you to be heard.
response.success_feedback: Really thoughtful opening. You changed the structure of the conversation before it even started, which changes everything that follows. That kind of intentionality is rare and powerful.

levels.title: Escalating a Concern to Leadership
levels.scenario: You have raised a concern about a process in your team three times through normal channels with no result. The issue is now affecting clients.

mcq.question: How do you escalate appropriately without burning bridges or appearing to go over your manager's head aggressively?
mcq.correct_option: Tell your manager you are planning to raise this with their manager given the client impact, explain your reasoning, and give them one final opportunity to resolve it first.
incorrect_options: Go directly to senior leadership without informing your manager first.
Document everything in a formal complaint to protect yourself before escalating.
Accept that the issue won't be resolved and find workarounds to manage the client impact yourself.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Transparency with your manager before escalating shows respect for the chain of command and gives them the chance to act — while making clear you will proceed.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either bypasses trust, becomes adversarial, or abandons accountability. Professional escalation is transparent, sequential, and outcome-focused. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to tell your manager you are planning to escalate this issue — professionally and transparently.
response.success_feedback: Handled with real integrity. You gave your manager notice, explained your reasoning, and made it about the outcome — not about going above their head. That's how professionals escalate.

levels.title: Telling Someone Their Actions Hurt You
levels.scenario: A close friend made a dismissive joke about something personal you shared with them. It really stung but they seem unaware of the impact.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to let them know their comment hurt you?
mcq.correct_option: Choose a calm private moment to mention it — name the specific comment, say how it landed for you, and give them the chance to respond before making any assumptions.
incorrect_options: Drop hints that something is wrong and wait for them to ask what's wrong.
Tell them in the heat of the moment that their comment was hurtful and unkind.
Decide it was probably a joke and they didn't mean it, so you shouldn't make it into a big deal.
mcq.correct_feedback: Really courageous. Specific, calm, and direct — with space for their perspective — is the only approach that gives the friendship a chance to grow through this.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes them guess, reacts emotionally, or dismisses something that genuinely mattered to you. Your feelings deserve to be named clearly and calmly. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to tell your friend how their comment affected you — clearly, calmly, and with care for the friendship.
response.success_feedback: That was real vulnerability with real dignity. You named it, explained it, and gave them a chance to understand. That conversation will make your friendship stronger.

levels.title: Closing a Difficult Conversation Well
levels.scenario: You have just had a hard but necessary conversation with a colleague about a tension that had been building between you. The air feels lighter but slightly fragile.

mcq.question: How do you close a difficult conversation in a way that feels complete and forward-facing?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge that this took courage from both sides, summarise the key things you've both agreed, and name one clear next step that you will both take to move forward.
incorrect_options: End it quickly with 'we're all good now, right?' and move on before the moment becomes uncomfortable.
Thank them for listening and exit without summarising anything in case it opens more discussion.
Tell them you hope things will be better from now on and leave the specifics vague.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent close! Acknowledging the bravery of both parties, summarising agreements, and anchoring a next step makes the conversation feel complete and sets a real path forward.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either rushes the ending, skips the landing, or leaves things too open-ended. A good close gives a difficult conversation its full meaning. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to close this difficult conversation in a way that feels complete, honest, and forward-facing.
response.success_feedback: What a strong landing. You honoured the conversation by closing it with intention — acknowledging both people, anchoring the agreements, and naming what comes next. That's how hard conversations become turning points.

levels.title: Opening a Presentation with Impact
levels.scenario: You are about to deliver a 20-minute presentation to a mixed audience of 30 people. You have 90 seconds to grab their attention.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to open a presentation?
mcq.correct_option: Open with a surprising statistic, a provocative question, or a short vivid story that is directly connected to the point of your talk — before introducing yourself or the agenda.
incorrect_options: Thank everyone for coming, introduce yourself in detail, and then outline the agenda before getting started.
Begin with an apology about being slightly nervous to show the audience you are approachable.
Open with a joke to warm up the room before transitioning to the serious content.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Leading with a hook — a story, question, or statistic — grabs attention before the audience has a chance to disengage.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either wastes the most precious moment with logistics, undermines your authority, or risks the joke not landing. Open with the thing that matters most — your hook. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the opening 60 seconds of your presentation — designed to hook the audience immediately.
response.success_feedback: That was a powerful opening! You grabbed the room before they even had a chance to drift. That first 60 seconds is everything — and you nailed it.

levels.title: Telling a Story to an Audience
levels.scenario: You are giving a presentation on workplace resilience and want to use a personal story to illustrate your central message. The audience of 50 professionals is listening.

mcq.question: What makes a personal story land effectively with a professional audience?
mcq.correct_option: Choose a story with a clear turning point, tell it in vivid specific detail, stay emotionally honest without oversharing, and make the link between the story and your message explicit.
incorrect_options: Choose the most dramatic thing that ever happened to you to ensure maximum impact.
Tell the story at length and trust the audience to draw their own conclusion about its relevance.
Keep the story brief and generic so no one in the audience feels it's too personal.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Specificity, honesty, and an explicit message link — that's the combination that makes a professional story land with power.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either prioritises drama over relevance, leaves the connection implicit, or is so vague it lacks emotional truth. A great story is specific, honest, and clearly connected to the point. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to tell your personal resilience story to this professional audience in a way that genuinely resonates.
response.success_feedback: Beautifully told! You chose the right details, stayed emotionally honest, and the link to your message was clear and powerful. That's the kind of story people carry home.

levels.title: Handling Tough Q&A Questions
levels.scenario: You have finished your presentation and a senior professional in the audience asks a sharp, challenging question that you weren't expecting.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to handle a tough question you weren't prepared for?
mcq.correct_option: Pause, thank them for the question, briefly restate it to buy yourself a moment to think, answer what you honestly can — and acknowledge clearly if part of it is outside your current knowledge.
incorrect_options: Deflect by saying 'Great question — we could do a whole talk on that' and then move to the next question.
Answer confidently even if you're not fully sure, to avoid appearing unprepared in front of the room.
Ask them what they think the answer is to turn the question back to the audience.
mcq.correct_feedback: Spot on! A pause, a restatement, an honest answer, and clear acknowledgment of limits — that's how composed experts handle tough Q&A.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either deflects without substance, risks spreading misinformation, or turns the spotlight back on the questioner inappropriately. Honesty and composure always wins. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to answer this challenging Q&A question with composure and intellectual honesty.
response.success_feedback: Handled brilliantly! You showed poise, gave what you genuinely could, and were honest about the limits. That kind of Q&A response builds more credibility than a polished deflection ever could.

levels.title: Contributing on a Panel
levels.scenario: You are one of four panellists at an industry conference. One panellist is dominating the conversation and the moderator is struggling to balance the discussion.

mcq.question: How do you contribute meaningfully without either staying silent or competing rudely for airtime?
mcq.correct_option: Wait for a natural opening, use a brief bridging phrase to signal you'd like to add to the point, make your contribution concise and distinctive, and defer clearly when done.
incorrect_options: Wait for the moderator to specifically call on you before contributing anything.
Cut in when the other panellist pauses for breath since that is the only way to be heard.
Address all your answers to the moderator and ignore the other panellists to avoid conflict.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! A bridging phrase, concise contribution, and a clear deferral — that's how you hold your own on a panel without dominating or disappearing.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either keeps you invisible, is disruptive, or creates a one-way dynamic. Panel contribution is an art of timing, brevity, and respect. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to enter the panel discussion and make a distinctive, concise contribution.
response.success_feedback: Excellent panel presence! You picked your moment, made a sharp point, and stepped back gracefully. That's the kind of panellist who gets invited back.

levels.title: Delivering an Inspiring Keynote
levels.scenario: You have been given 15 minutes to deliver a keynote at a professional conference on a subject you are deeply passionate about.

mcq.question: What is the single most important thing to get right in a keynote address?
mcq.correct_option: Have one clear, memorable central idea that the entire talk builds toward — every story, data point, and example should serve that single idea.
incorrect_options: Cover as many relevant insights as possible to maximise the value delivered to the audience.
Make sure your slides are visually polished and comprehensive so they support everything you say.
Rehearse until your delivery is smooth and professional, since presence and polish are what audiences remember.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! One clear idea, consistently reinforced — that's what makes a keynote stick in memory. More ideas dilute the impact, not increase it.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either sacrifices depth for breadth, leans on slides over substance, or mistakes polish for resonance. The most memorable talks have one clear thing to say. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the opening and central idea of your keynote in a way that immediately anchors the entire talk.
response.success_feedback: Brilliant! You stated your central idea with clarity and conviction right from the start. Everything else in your keynote now has a spine to hang on. That's how great talks are built.

levels.title: Recovering from Losing Your Place
levels.scenario: You are mid-presentation and you lose your thread completely. You can see people starting to notice the pause.

mcq.question: What is the best way to recover from losing your place in a presentation?
mcq.correct_option: Take a calm breath, acknowledge the pause without excessive apology, glance at your notes if needed, and pick up from the last clear point — the audience will respect your composure.
incorrect_options: Apologise profusely and explain that you're nervous, to show the audience you are self-aware.
Skip the section you lost and jump ahead to the next clear point on your slides.
Ask the audience where you were up to, turning the recovery into an interactive moment.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! A calm breath, a brief natural pause, and picking back up — the audience remembers how you handled it, not that it happened.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes the moment bigger than it is, creates a visible gap, or makes the audience do work that's your job. Composure is the recovery. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to recover from losing your thread mid-presentation — smoothly, calmly, and with presence.
response.success_feedback: Smooth and composed recovery! The audience saw someone who handles imperfection with grace — and that is actually more impressive than a flawless delivery.

levels.title: Using Humour Effectively
levels.scenario: You want to open a formal presentation with a touch of humour to warm up the room, but you are concerned about landing it well with a diverse professional audience.

mcq.question: What kind of humour works best in a professional speaking context?
mcq.correct_option: Use self-deprecating or observational humour tied to the topic, keep it brief, and ensure it could not reasonably be seen as at the expense of any group of people.
incorrect_options: Use a topical current events joke since it will feel fresh and culturally connected.
Open with a joke you've used before at social gatherings that always gets a laugh.
Avoid humour entirely in a formal setting since it risks damaging your professional credibility.
