mcq.correct_feedback: Spot on! Self-deprecating or observational humour that connects to your topic, and includes no one, is reliably safe and warm.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either risks alienating some of the audience, relies on context that may not transfer, or abandons a tool that, used well, is genuinely powerful. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open your professional presentation with a brief, well-chosen moment of humour.
response.success_feedback: Perfectly landed! Your humour was inclusive, relevant, and brief — it warmed the room without risking anything. That's the art of professional comedy.

levels.title: Giving a Toast
levels.scenario: You have been asked to give a toast at your colleague's farewell dinner. Around 20 people are present, including senior leaders and close friends of the person leaving.

mcq.question: What makes a memorable, well-received professional toast?
mcq.correct_option: Keep it under two minutes, share one specific story or quality that captures who they truly are, end with a genuine, warm wish — and raise your glass with conviction.
incorrect_options: List all of their achievements and contributions in detail so the full impact of their departure is clear.
Tell a funny story you know they find embarrassing to show how well you know them.
Keep it general and complimentary so that everyone in the room can relate to what you're saying.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Specific, brief, warm, and ending with conviction — that's the toast structure that makes people emotional in the best way.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either becomes a CV summary, risks humiliating them, or is so generic it could be for anyone. The best toast is short, specific, and from the heart. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver your toast to this departing colleague — warm, specific, and memorable.
response.success_feedback: Beautiful toast! You captured something real about them, kept it the right length, and ended it with feeling. That's a toast worth remembering.

levels.title: Making Data Come Alive
levels.scenario: Your presentation contains a complex set of data showing a 47% drop in customer retention over 18 months. The audience is non-technical.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to present this data to a non-technical audience?
mcq.correct_option: Translate the number into a human reality — 'Nearly half the customers we had 18 months ago are no longer with us' — and then show the chart as supporting evidence, not the centrepiece.
incorrect_options: Display the full data set with all supporting metrics so the audience can see the full picture.
Walk through the methodology behind the data collection first to establish credibility.
Present the statistic alone with a clear visual and trust the audience to understand its significance.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Human translation first, chart as support — that's how you make data land with non-technical audiences.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either overwhelms with data, delays the point, or leaves the translation work to an audience that may not do it. Always humanise the number before showing the chart. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to present this customer retention data to a non-technical audience in a way that makes the impact immediately clear.
response.success_feedback: Brilliantly communicated! You made the number human before showing it — and that's why it will stay with the audience long after they've forgotten the slide.

levels.title: Closing with a Call to Action
levels.scenario: You are wrapping up a 20-minute presentation designed to persuade your audience to change a specific behaviour. Your final 60 seconds is the most important.

mcq.question: What does a powerful presentation closing include?
mcq.correct_option: Briefly restate the central message, make the desired action specific and achievable, create a sense of genuine urgency or meaning, and end on a phrase that resonates emotionally.
incorrect_options: Summarise all the main points of the presentation so the audience remembers everything you covered.
Thank the audience for their time and open the floor to any final questions.
End with an inspiring quote from a well-known figure to leave the audience on a high.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Central message restated, specific action, urgency or meaning, and an emotionally resonant final line — that's a close worth remembering.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either restates too much, ends on process rather than punch, or borrows someone else's words when yours would be more powerful. End with intention and specificity. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the final 60 seconds of your presentation — a close that moves the audience to act.
response.success_feedback: What a finish! You restated the core idea, made the ask specific, gave them a reason it matters now, and landed on a phrase that will stick. That's how you leave a room changed.

levels.title: Negotiating a Salary Increase
levels.scenario: You have been in your role for two years, consistently outperformed your targets, and taken on significantly more responsibility. Your review is tomorrow.

mcq.question: What is the most effective strategy for negotiating a salary increase?
mcq.correct_option: Come in with a specific number anchored to market data and your demonstrated contribution, state it with confidence, and be prepared to discuss trade-offs rather than back down immediately.
incorrect_options: Ask what the company can offer and negotiate upward from whatever they say.
Lead by telling your manager you need more money to cover your increasing living costs.
State a vague desire for 'more recognition' and let the manager propose a number.
mcq.correct_feedback: Strong approach! A specific, evidence-based number stated with confidence sets the anchor and makes the conversation concrete from the start.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either cedes the anchor, frames the ask around personal need rather than professional value, or is too vague to negotiate from. Negotiate from value and specificity. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to make your salary negotiation ask — with confidence, specificity, and supporting evidence.
response.success_feedback: Really well negotiated! You anchored with a specific number, backed it with your contribution, and stayed composed. That's how professionals negotiate their worth.

levels.title: Negotiating with a Vendor
levels.scenario: You are in a commercial negotiation with a supplier who has quoted a price 25% above your budget. The product is important but not irreplaceable.

mcq.question: What negotiation technique gives you the most leverage in this situation?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge that you value their product, name your budget constraint directly, and signal that you have a credible alternative — then ask what they can do given your constraints.
incorrect_options: Tell them their price is far too high and you expect a much better offer or you'll leave.
Accept their offer and negotiate extras or additional deliverables to make up the difference in value.
Make up a lower competing quote that doesn't exist to force them to match it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Excellent! Valuing the relationship, being transparent about your constraint, and referencing alternatives without bluffing — that's principled negotiation.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either creates unnecessary confrontation, leaves money on the table, or risks your credibility if the bluff is called. Transparent leverage always outperforms aggression or dishonesty. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to negotiate the vendor's pricing within your budget constraints — professionally and with leverage.
response.success_feedback: Strong negotiation! You were transparent about your constraints, signalled real alternatives, and kept the relationship intact. That's commercial communication at its best.

levels.title: Closing a Partnership Deal
levels.scenario: You are in a final meeting to close a strategic partnership agreement. The other party has been engaged but keeps asking for additional time to 'run it past their team'.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to close this deal in the final meeting?
mcq.correct_option: Summarise the agreed terms confidently, address any remaining uncertainty directly, and ask clearly what would need to be true for them to move forward today.
incorrect_options: Give them the additional time they're requesting and wait for them to come back when ready.
Apply pressure by telling them the terms on the table will not be available after this week.
Ask them to tell you their remaining concerns and then promise to follow up with answers by email.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Summarising, addressing uncertainty, and asking what needs to be true to close today — that's a professional close that respects the relationship.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either loses momentum, uses pressure that may backfire, or delays again. The close question is the most powerful tool in negotiation. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to make your closing move in this partnership negotiation and bring the deal home.
response.success_feedback: That close was smooth and confident! You summarised, removed the last uncertainty, and asked the right question to unlock the decision. That's how deals get done.

levels.title: Negotiating Cross-Culturally
levels.scenario: You are in a business negotiation with a counterpart from a culture where direct disagreement is considered disrespectful, and relationship-building precedes any deal discussion.

mcq.question: How should you adapt your negotiation approach in this cultural context?
mcq.correct_option: Invest genuinely in relationship-building first, allow more time than you might normally for the deal to develop, ask questions rather than pushing positions, and read indirect signals as carefully as direct ones.
incorrect_options: Proceed with your normal direct negotiation style and trust that the quality of your offer will speak for itself.
Ask them explicitly at the start of the meeting how they prefer to negotiate so you can adapt.
Speak slowly and avoid using idioms or cultural references to ensure they understand you clearly.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Cultural negotiation requires genuine adaptation, patience, and reading both what is said and what is not. Relationship comes before deal in many cultures.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either ignores cultural context, creates an awkward meta-conversation, or addresses only language rather than the deeper norms. True cross-cultural competence is in the approach, not just the words. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open this cross-cultural negotiation meeting in a way that builds trust before discussing business.
response.success_feedback: Really culturally intelligent! You prioritised the relationship over the agenda, which is exactly what creates the conditions for a successful deal in this context. That's sophisticated communication.

levels.title: Breaking a Deadlock
levels.scenario: Your negotiation has stalled. Both sides have restated their positions multiple times and there is no movement. The meeting has been going for two hours.

mcq.question: What is the most effective technique for breaking a negotiation deadlock?
mcq.correct_option: Shift the conversation away from positions toward underlying interests — ask what they are ultimately trying to achieve — and see if a creative option can serve both needs.
incorrect_options: Restate your position more firmly one final time and make clear you won't be moving further.
Suggest taking a break and reconvening tomorrow to let both sides cool down.
Make a small concession to show goodwill and hope they reciprocate enough to get things moving.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Moving from positions to interests is the most proven technique for unlocking deadlocks. The solution is almost never in the stated positions.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either hardens the impasse, delays without addressing the cause, or trades value without insight. The breakthrough comes from understanding the why behind the what. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to shift this deadlocked negotiation by exploring the interests beneath the positions.
response.success_feedback: That was a masterful pivot! You moved the conversation from 'what we each want' to 'why we each want it' — and that shift is where every negotiation breakthrough lives.

levels.title: Making a Strategic Concession
levels.scenario: You are mid-negotiation and you need to offer a concession to keep things moving, but you want to ensure you get value back in return.

mcq.question: What is the most strategic way to offer a concession in a negotiation?
mcq.correct_option: Make the concession conditional — 'If you can move on X, I can look at offering Y' — and frame the concession as significant even if it costs you relatively little.
incorrect_options: Offer the concession freely as a gesture of good faith without asking for anything in return.
Only concede after they have pushed back multiple times so it doesn't look too easy.
Make several small concessions in quick succession to show flexibility and close the deal faster.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Conditional concessions create reciprocity, and framing the concession well maximises its perceived value.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either gives value away for free, delays unnecessarily, or depletes your negotiating currency too quickly. Never give without getting — and always frame what you give as significant. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to offer your strategic concession in a way that creates reciprocal movement from the other side.
response.success_feedback: Strategically sharp! You gave conditionally, framed the concession well, and created a structure for the other party to match you. That's negotiation with intelligence.

levels.title: Walking Away from a Bad Deal
levels.scenario: After weeks of negotiation, it is clear the terms on offer do not meet your needs and are unlikely to improve. You need to walk away.

mcq.question: What is the most professional way to exit a negotiation that isn't working?
mcq.correct_option: State clearly and calmly that the current terms don't work for you, thank them for the time invested, and leave the door open by saying you hope circumstances allow for a different conversation in the future.
incorrect_options: Make one more push with a significantly improved offer to see if there is any movement before leaving.
Tell them you're disappointed in their inflexibility and that you expected better from them.
Agree to the bad terms with the intention of renegotiating them once the relationship is established.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Calm, clear, and doors-open — a professional walkaway protects your interests and preserves the relationship for future possibilities.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either chases bad terms, burns the bridge, or enters the relationship with hidden intentions. A clean, professional walkaway is sometimes the best outcome. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to walk away from this negotiation professionally, firmly, and without burning the bridge.
response.success_feedback: Executed with real class. You named the gap, kept your dignity, and left the future open. Sometimes walking away with grace is the strongest thing a negotiator can do.

levels.title: Navigating a Power Imbalance
levels.scenario: You are negotiating a contract renewal with a client who is significantly larger than your company and knows it. They are using their leverage aggressively.

mcq.question: How do you negotiate effectively when the other party has significantly more power?
mcq.correct_option: Establish your best alternative clearly in your own mind, focus the conversation on the specific value you uniquely provide, and avoid conceding under pressure alone.
incorrect_options: Accept the imbalance and make generous concessions early to build goodwill with a powerful client.
Match their aggressive posture to show you are not intimidated by their leverage.
Delay the negotiation to buy time and hope the power dynamic shifts in your favour.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Knowing your alternative, emphasising unique value, and holding through pressure — those are the tools of a negotiator who doesn't need to win the power game to win the deal.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either concedes too early, escalates into a dynamic you'll lose, or avoids the conversation. Your power in any negotiation is your value and your alternative. Lean into those. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to assert your value and hold your position in this high-power-imbalance negotiation.
response.success_feedback: Impressively composed! You didn't flinch at the power play — you redirected to value. That's the most effective strategy when you're the smaller party at the table.

levels.title: Re-opening a Negotiation
levels.scenario: You agreed to terms three weeks ago but have since discovered that circumstances have changed significantly, making the original terms untenable for your side.

mcq.question: How do you re-open a negotiation that has already been agreed without destroying the relationship?
mcq.correct_option: Reach out promptly, be fully transparent about what has changed and why, acknowledge the inconvenience directly, and come with a specific, reasonable proposal rather than just opening it back up.
incorrect_options: Draft legal correspondence to formally challenge the original terms based on changed circumstances.
Wait to see if the situation improves before raising the issue, to avoid unnecessary conflict.
Tell them you've found a problem with the original agreement without revealing the full context.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Transparency, swift communication, genuine acknowledgment, and a concrete proposal shows good faith — the foundation for successfully re-opening any agreement.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either escalates immediately, delays a conversation that needs to happen, or withholds information that erodes trust. Honesty and a real proposal are essential here. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to re-open this agreed negotiation with full transparency and a concrete new proposal.
response.success_feedback: Handled with integrity. You didn't hide the situation, you owned the awkwardness, and you came with a solution not just a problem. That's how you protect relationships even when agreements need to change.

levels.title: Turning a No Into a Yes
levels.scenario: A potential partner has declined your proposal. The conversation was positive but they said the timing isn't right. You believe the opportunity is real.

mcq.question: What is the best way to respond to a 'not right now' from a potential partner?
mcq.correct_option: Thank them for considering it, ask what specifically would need to be different for them to reconsider — then agree to return with a proposal that addresses those conditions.
incorrect_options: Push back immediately by explaining why now is actually the perfect time for them.
Accept the rejection and move on, since following up risks damaging the relationship.
Offer a heavily discounted version of the proposal to make it easier to say yes right now.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Understanding their specific conditions for a yes turns a no into a roadmap — and shows a level of professional patience that impresses.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either argues with their timing instinct, gives up on a real opportunity, or discounts the value unnecessarily. A 'no for now' is only final if you treat it as final. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this 'not right now' in a way that keeps the door open and maps a path back to yes.
response.success_feedback: Brilliant! You didn't accept the no as final or fight it — you made it a starting point for a future yes. That's negotiation patience at its finest.

levels.title: Communicating Urgency in an Emergency
levels.scenario: A fire alarm has gone off in your office building and you are the most senior person on the floor. People are looking to you for direction.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to communicate in this kind of high-stakes emergency?
mcq.correct_option: Speak in a loud, calm, and clear voice. Give one instruction at a time. Do not show panic. Lead people toward the exit and account for everyone.
incorrect_options: Tell everyone to stay calm and wait for official instructions before moving.
Shout to get everyone's attention and then give all the instructions at once.
Leave immediately and trust that others will figure out what to do without guidance.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Calm, loud clarity with one instruction at a time is how you lead effectively when others are panicking.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either delays action, overwhelms people under pressure, or abandons your responsibility. Clear, calm, sequential instruction is the gold standard. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to give the instructions to safely evacuate your floor — calmly, clearly, and with leadership.
response.success_feedback: That was genuine crisis leadership. You stayed calm, communicated clearly, and gave people exactly what they needed — direction. That presence saves lives.

levels.title: Addressing a Public-Facing Crisis
levels.scenario: Your company has been linked in a media story to a significant data breach affecting thousands of customers. You need to address it publicly within the hour.

mcq.question: What should a responsible public statement in a crisis prioritise?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge what has happened factually, express genuine concern for those affected, state what is being done immediately, and commit to keeping the public informed as more is known.
incorrect_options: Release a statement through legal that denies specific allegations and avoids confirming details.
Wait until you have the full picture so you can issue a complete, accurate statement rather than a partial one.
Redirect focus to the company's positive track record and history of responsible data handling.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Acknowledgment, empathy, action, and transparency — in that order — is the only framework that holds credibility in a public crisis.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either denies what needs to be owned, delays when speed is critical, or deflects when acknowledgment is required. In a crisis, transparency is your only asset. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the key message in your public crisis statement on behalf of your organisation.
response.success_feedback: Handled with real accountability. You acknowledged, showed empathy, named the action, and committed to transparency. That's the statement that begins to restore trust.

levels.title: Responding to a Hostile Audience
levels.scenario: You are presenting a cost-cutting initiative to a group of employees whose roles may be affected. Several people are visibly angry and interrupting.

mcq.question: How do you maintain control and credibility when faced with a hostile audience?
mcq.correct_option: Pause, acknowledge their frustration directly and genuinely, invite one person to voice their concern fully, and then respond to the substance — not the emotion — before continuing.
incorrect_options: Power through the presentation and address questions at the end when emotions have settled.
Apologise for the decisions being made and distance yourself from responsibility for them.
Ask security to remove the most disruptive attendees so the meeting can proceed professionally.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Acknowledgment, invitation, and substance-focused response — that's how you hold a hostile room without fighting it.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either ignores real emotion, undermines your authority, or escalates to a security issue unnecessarily. Stand in the storm with acknowledgment — it disarms hostility faster than anything. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to acknowledge the hostility in the room and begin to redirect it toward a constructive conversation.
response.success_feedback: That was remarkable presence under pressure. You didn't run from the emotion — you walked into it and gave it a voice. That is how you turn a hostile room into a heard one.

levels.title: Thinking on Your Feet
levels.scenario: You are giving a presentation when a senior executive asks you a detailed question you have no prepared answer for. Everyone is watching.

mcq.question: What is the most effective strategy for thinking on your feet under pressure?
mcq.correct_option: Pause briefly without apology, repeat the question to buy a moment of thinking time, answer the parts you can with confidence, and be honest about what you will follow up on.
incorrect_options: Fill the silence immediately with words to avoid looking like you don't know the answer.
Tell them it's a great question that deserves more thought and promise to send a full answer later.
Ask them to come back to you at the end of the session so you can gather your thoughts.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! A deliberate pause, restating the question, confident partial answer, and honest follow-up — that's how composure is built under fire.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either fills silence with noise, uses a phrase that feels evasive, or postpones the whole thing unnecessarily. Pause, restate, answer what you can, follow up the rest. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this unexpected senior question with composure and credibility.
response.success_feedback: Brilliantly handled! You paused, thought, answered with confidence where you could, and committed to follow up on the rest. That's not weakness — that's mastery.

levels.title: Handling a Journalist's Difficult Question
levels.scenario: You are representing your company in a media interview and a journalist asks a pointed question about a recent decision that caused public controversy.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to handle a difficult question from a journalist?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the concern behind the question, answer honestly within the limits of what you can share, and bridge to the context or action your organisation is taking.
incorrect_options: Refuse to answer and tell the journalist that the question is outside the scope of today's interview.
Answer in very long sentences that contain so much complexity the key point gets buried.
Repeat your prepared talking points without directly addressing the question, hoping they move on.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Acknowledgment, honest limited answer, and a bridge to context — that's the professional formula for media communication that holds credibility.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either creates a bigger story, obscures the response, or is transparent to any experienced journalist. Acknowledge, answer honestly, bridge forward. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this journalist's pointed question with composure, honesty, and professionalism.
response.success_feedback: Really professionally handled! You acknowledged the concern, answered within appropriate limits, and gave context. That's the kind of media response that holds up.

levels.title: Managing a PR Crisis Online
levels.scenario: A tweet criticising your organisation has gone viral with thousands of shares. The comments are full of angry customers. You manage the company's social channels.

mcq.question: What is the right approach to a social media PR crisis?
mcq.correct_option: Respond quickly with a genuine, human acknowledgment — avoid corporate language — take responsibility where due, and communicate what specific action is being taken.
incorrect_options: Delete the original post being criticised so the misinformation can't spread further.
Do not respond publicly — issue a statement on your website and wait for the storm to pass.
Respond to every critical comment individually using a standard template to show you're responsive.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! A swift, human, specific and accountable response is the only thing that can stop a social media crisis from accelerating.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either fans the flames, removes you from the public conversation people are having, or feels robotic and insincere. Speed, humanity, and accountability — that's the formula. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to draft the public social media response that will begin to turn this crisis around.
response.success_feedback: That response was fast, human, and accountable. You didn't hide behind corporate language — you showed up as a real organisation that cares. That's what people need to see in a crisis.

levels.title: Steadying Your Team in Upheaval
levels.scenario: Your company has just announced a major reorganisation. Your team is anxious and rumours are spreading. You need to address them before the official communication arrives.

mcq.question: What is the right thing to do for your team right now?
mcq.correct_option: Bring the team together, acknowledge the uncertainty and how unsettling it is, share what you actually know, and commit clearly to passing on information as it arrives.
incorrect_options: Tell the team you've heard the rumours but don't have information to share yet, and ask them to wait for official comms.
Reassure them everything will be fine and none of their roles are at risk to prevent panic.
Tell them to focus on their work and not get distracted by rumours that might not be accurate.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Gathering the team, validating the anxiety, sharing what you know, and committing to transparency — that's how you lead in the fog.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either withholds connection, makes promises you can't keep, or dismisses legitimate concern. In uncertainty, your team needs your presence before they need your answers. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address your team in this moment of organisational uncertainty — honestly and with steadying leadership.
response.success_feedback: That was real leadership in hard conditions. You gathered your people, acknowledged reality, and made a commitment to them. That's what keeps teams together when organisations shake.

levels.title: Adapting Your Message on the Fly
levels.scenario: You have arrived to deliver a presentation to a group of 20 clients and the projector has failed. Your talk relied heavily on slides. You have 2 minutes to adapt.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to handle this unexpected situation?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the technical issue briefly with a light touch, state that you'll deliver the session without slides, briefly remap the structure aloud for the audience, and proceed with full confidence.
incorrect_options: Delay the session until the technical issue can be resolved rather than deliver a substandard version.
Apologise repeatedly throughout the talk for not being able to show the slides.
Read directly from your notes since the slides were your memory prompts.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! A brief light acknowledgment, a verbal map of the session, and full confidence forward — that's how pros handle equipment failure.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either delays unnecessarily, undermines your credibility throughout, or produces a flat delivery. The slides were never the talk — you were. Own it. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open your presentation without slides — confidently and without making the technical failure the centrepiece.
response.success_feedback: What an impressive response to adversity! You turned a technical failure into a display of real expertise and composure. That audience just saw something more valuable than any slide deck.

levels.title: Communicating Failure to Stakeholders
levels.scenario: A major initiative you led and championed has significantly underperformed against its objectives. You must present the results to a board of senior stakeholders.

mcq.question: What is the most credible way to communicate a high-profile failure to senior stakeholders?
mcq.correct_option: Lead with the facts — what happened and by how much it fell short — take clear responsibility without excessive self-flagellation, explain what you've learned, and present a concrete path forward.
incorrect_options: Open with all the things that went well before addressing the shortfall to put it in context.
Distribute blame appropriately across the various factors and teams that contributed to the result.
Focus primarily on what you will do differently next time rather than dwelling on what went wrong.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Facts first, ownership, learning, and path forward — that's the structure of a failure communication that preserves credibility with a demanding audience.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either leads with spin, spreads blame, or avoids the full accounting the board needs. Senior stakeholders respect unflinching honesty far more than managed framing. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to present this failed initiative to the board — with honesty, ownership, and a clear path forward.
response.success_feedback: That was a masterclass in accountability. You didn't hide from the numbers, you owned what happened, and you gave the board a reason to trust you with what comes next. That's rare courage.

levels.title: Rebuilding Credibility After a Crisis
levels.scenario: Following a public crisis that damaged your organisation's reputation, you are giving your first public address to rebuild trust. The audience is sceptical.

mcq.question: What is the most important thing your communication must demonstrate in this moment?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the full truth of what happened without minimisation, demonstrate specific and verifiable changes you have made, and speak with humility rather than defensiveness.
incorrect_options: Focus on your organisation's past record and the good it has done to rebalance the narrative.
Emphasise how much you have suffered as an organisation to show that consequences have already been felt.
Announce a series of ambitious new commitments that signal you are moving in a new direction.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Trust is rebuilt through full truth, verifiable change, and humility — not reframing, self-pity, or forward promises that haven't been earned yet.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either deflects, appeals for sympathy, or makes promises before proof. The only thing that rebuilds credibility is honest acknowledgment plus demonstrated change. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver the opening of your trust-rebuilding address — with full honesty and genuine humility.
response.success_feedback: That was a profoundly powerful opening. You didn't defend or deflect — you acknowledged and showed change. That's the only foundation on which credibility can be rebuilt. Remarkable.

levels.title: Reading the Room
levels.scenario: You walk into a team meeting and notice the energy is unusually tense. Two people who were close colleagues are not making eye contact. You are about to launch your planned agenda.

mcq.question: What is the most emotionally intelligent response to this room dynamic?
mcq.correct_option: Pause before launching into the agenda. Acknowledge the energy you're sensing with a light, open question — giving the room a moment to breathe before proceeding.
incorrect_options: Launch straight into the agenda as planned since the meeting content is time-sensitive.
Address the tension directly by asking the two colleagues what is going on between them.
Reschedule the meeting since it's clear the team isn't in the right headspace for productive work.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Reading the room and giving it a moment to breathe shows high EQ and often leads to a more productive meeting than bulldozing through.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either ignores the dynamic, escalates it, or overreacts to it. A light acknowledgment and brief pause is usually all a tense room needs. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to acknowledge the room's energy at the start of this meeting in a way that is light, observant, and helpful.
response.success_feedback: Beautiful room-reading! That brief pause and acknowledgment probably shifted the energy more than any agenda item could. That's the quiet power of emotional intelligence.

levels.title: Regulating Your Emotions in Conflict
levels.scenario: During a heated professional discussion, you feel genuine anger rising — your jaw is tight and you can feel yourself becoming reactive.

mcq.question: What is the most emotionally intelligent response when you feel anger rising in a professional setting?
mcq.correct_option: Slow your breathing deliberately, lower your voice rather than raising it, and if needed, name the intensity calmly: 'I feel strongly about this — let me take a moment to make sure I respond well.'
incorrect_options: Express your frustration clearly so the other person understands the seriousness of the issue.
Excuse yourself from the conversation immediately without explanation until you have cooled down.
Push the anger down and continue speaking as normally as possible so no one notices.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Naming your emotional state with calm language is far more powerful and professional than either expressing or suppressing it.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either lets the emotion drive the conversation, removes you without context, or bottles something that will affect your quality of communication. Self-regulation is the key skill here. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to manage this moment of rising anger in the conversation — with self-awareness and emotional regulation.
response.success_feedback: Impressive self-regulation! You didn't suppress it, you named it — and in doing so, you kept the conversation professional and yourself credible. That's emotional intelligence in action.

levels.title: Responding to Grief with Compassion
levels.scenario: A close colleague tells you that their parent passed away last week. They are back at work and seem to be managing, but they brought it up to you personally.

mcq.question: What is the most compassionate and appropriate response?
mcq.correct_option: Express your genuine condolences, acknowledge the weight of what they're carrying, and follow their lead — offer support in specific ways and let them set the tone for how much they want to discuss.
incorrect_options: Tell them that their parent is in a better place and that time will help heal the grief.
Share a story of losing someone you were close to so they know they are not alone.
Quickly acknowledge it and move on to avoid making them feel uncomfortable by dwelling on it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. Genuine condolences, acknowledgment of the weight, and following their lead — that's compassionate support that honours their grief without taking it over.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either minimises with platitudes, redirects to your own experience, or rushes past one of the most significant moments a colleague might share with you. Sit in it with them, however briefly. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to your colleague's bereavement with genuine compassion and the right amount of space.
response.success_feedback: That response was full of humanity. You didn't rush, you didn't solve, you didn't redirect — you just showed up for them. That's all grief needs from another person.

levels.title: Dealing with Passive-Aggressive Behaviour
levels.scenario: A colleague keeps responding to your requests with comments like 'fine, if that's what you want' and 'I suppose I can fit that in' in a tone that communicates clear displeasure.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to address passive-aggressive behaviour?
mcq.correct_option: Name what you are noticing — calmly and without accusation — and invite them to share directly if something is bothering them, making it clear you'd rather hear it straight.
incorrect_options: Respond to the surface words as if the tone doesn't exist to avoid encouraging the behaviour.
Mirror their tone back to signal that you've noticed and that it's unwelcome.
Report the behaviour to your manager to create a record before it escalates further.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Calmly naming the pattern and inviting directness is the most effective and emotionally intelligent way to address passive-aggression.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either reinforces the dynamic, escalates it, or skips a direct conversation that could resolve it quickly. Name it, invite directness, and give them the space to speak honestly. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address the passive-aggressive dynamic with your colleague in a calm, direct, and non-accusatory way.
response.success_feedback: Really skilfully handled! You named the pattern without attacking the person, and you created an opening for honesty. Most passive-aggressive dynamics dissolve when directness is genuinely invited.

levels.title: Addressing Someone's Anxiety
levels.scenario: A team member comes to you clearly anxious about an upcoming high-stakes presentation they have to give to senior leadership for the first time.

mcq.question: What is the most helpful and emotionally intelligent response?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge that it makes sense to feel nervous, normalise it as something even experienced presenters feel, and ask what specific part of it they are most anxious about — then help with that.
incorrect_options: Tell them there's nothing to worry about since they are well prepared and will be fine.
Share that you were also anxious the first time you presented to senior leadership.
Immediately offer to run through the presentation with them so they feel more prepared.
mcq.correct_feedback: Spot on! Normalising the anxiety, asking where it lives specifically, and addressing that specific thing is far more helpful than reassurance or your own story.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either dismisses the feeling, redirects to your experience, or jumps to practical solutions before emotional acknowledgment. Always name the feeling before fixing the situation. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to help your team member with their pre-presentation anxiety in a genuinely supportive way.
response.success_feedback: Beautifully done. You acknowledged the feeling as legitimate, normalised it, and then targeted your help at the specific fear. That's emotional support with practical intelligence.

levels.title: Opening a Mental Health Conversation
levels.scenario: You manage a team member who has been showing signs of significant stress — coming in late, making uncharacteristic errors, and withdrawing from the group. You want to check in.

mcq.question: How do you open a conversation about mental health with a team member sensitively and professionally?
mcq.correct_option: Find a private space, share the specific changes you have observed without labelling or diagnosing, express genuine concern, and ask an open question — 'I wanted to check in — how are you actually doing?'
incorrect_options: Ask them directly if they're experiencing any mental health issues so you can understand how best to support them.
Tell them their performance has been declining and ask what's going on before connecting it to your concern for them.
Suggest they speak to HR or the company's Employee Assistance Programme without having the conversation yourself.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Observational, private, caring, and open — that's how you create the conditions for someone to feel safe enough to be honest.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either labels too quickly, leads with performance rather than care, or outsources a human conversation that needs to come from you first. Observation, care, and openness — in that order. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to check in on your team member in a private, caring, and sensitive way.
response.success_feedback: That was a remarkable act of leadership. You created safety through observation and care — not labels or performance-talk. That team member just felt genuinely seen by someone who has real responsibility over them.

levels.title: Balancing Empathy with Accountability
levels.scenario: A team member who has been going through a difficult personal period has missed a critical deadline that has impacted a client. They are clearly distressed.

mcq.question: How do you hold someone accountable while still showing genuine empathy?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge their personal situation with genuine care, then separately and gently name the impact of the missed deadline, and discuss together what support and what next steps are needed.
incorrect_options: Focus fully on the personal situation right now since accountability can be addressed when they are in a better place.
Address the deadline impact directly and make it clear that personal circumstances cannot affect professional responsibilities.
Send a written message covering both elements rather than having a verbal conversation during such an emotional time.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Empathy then accountability — each given full weight, handled separately — is how a leader holds both the human and the professional standard at once.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either defers accountability too long, dismisses the human element, or avoids the directness that the person and the situation deserve. Both empathy and accountability are required — and in the right sequence. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to hold this conversation that balances genuine care for your team member with clear accountability for the missed deadline.
response.success_feedback: That was extraordinarily well balanced. You held the person and the standard at the same time — and that is one of the hardest things a leader is asked to do. Beautifully handled.

levels.title: Managing Your Patience
levels.scenario: A colleague keeps asking you the same basic questions despite having been given the answers repeatedly. You are frustrated but need to maintain the professional relationship.

mcq.question: What is the most emotionally intelligent response to this ongoing frustration?
mcq.correct_option: Address the root issue — ask how they prefer to receive information, create a resource for them to reference, and gently name that you'd like them to try that first before coming to you.
incorrect_options: Answer the question again patiently and trust that eventually it will sink in.
Express your frustration directly so they understand the impact their repeated questions have on your time.
Start becoming less responsive to their messages so they learn to be more self-sufficient.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Fixing the system — preferred learning format and a self-reference resource — is more compassionate and effective than either enduring or expressing frustration.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either enables the pattern, escalates with emotion, or uses passive withdrawal instead of direct communication. The most emotionally intelligent response addresses the cause, not the symptom. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address this situation with your colleague in a way that solves the pattern rather than just managing it.
response.success_feedback: Really smart and emotionally regulated response! You found the root cause, proposed a solution that helps both of you, and kept the relationship intact. That's what high EQ looks like in a practical situation.

levels.title: Accepting Criticism with Openness
levels.scenario: A colleague gives you direct, unsolicited feedback that a recent piece of work you were proud of was unclear and difficult to follow. You feel stung.

mcq.question: What is the most emotionally intelligent response to this feedback?
mcq.correct_option: Take a breath, thank them sincerely for telling you, ask one or two specific questions to understand what wasn't clear, and commit to reviewing it with their feedback in mind.
incorrect_options: Explain the thinking behind the work so they can understand why you made the choices you did.
Tell them you'll pass the feedback on to your manager and see what they think.
Agree politely in the moment but dismiss the feedback internally since you disagree with their assessment.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Gratitude, curiosity, and commitment — that's the anatomy of a genuinely open response to feedback that stings.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either gets defensive, deflects responsibility, or is dishonest. Accepting feedback openly is a discipline, and one of the most valuable professional habits you can build. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to respond to this unsolicited critical feedback with genuine openness — even though it stings.
response.success_feedback: That was genuinely impressive openness. You thanked them, got curious, and committed to reflect. Most people can't do that when they're stung — but you did. That's real professional maturity.

levels.title: Being Vulnerable at Work
levels.scenario: You are in a team meeting and your manager asks everyone to share one thing they find challenging about their current role. You feel the instinct to give a polished non-answer.

mcq.question: What is the most emotionally intelligent choice in this moment?
mcq.correct_option: Share something real — a genuine challenge, framed professionally — that shows honest self-awareness without oversharing or performing vulnerability.
incorrect_options: Share something that sounds like a challenge but is actually a strength in disguise, to seem self-aware without real exposure.
Pass and say you're broadly happy with your role and don't want to take up others' time.
Share the most significant challenge you're facing in raw emotional detail to show full honesty.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Real vulnerability — professionally framed and honestly felt — is what builds true psychological safety in a team. It's also what earns you genuine respect.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either stays in performance mode, removes yourself from the moment, or overshares. Vulnerable and professional can exist in the same moment — and that's the sweet spot. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to share a genuine professional challenge in this team meeting — honestly and with appropriate openness.
response.success_feedback: That was real and brave. You gave something true — not performed. And in doing so, you probably gave someone else in that room permission to do the same. That's the gift of genuine vulnerability.

levels.title: Commanding Attention When You Enter a Room
levels.scenario: You are the most senior person attending a high-stakes meeting with external partners. As you enter, the room hasn't fully settled yet.

mcq.question: What communicates the strongest executive presence as you enter a room?
mcq.correct_option: Enter at a measured pace, make brief eye contact with people as you move to your seat, greet individuals by name where you can, and let the room settle before speaking.
incorrect_options: Move quickly to your seat and immediately start the meeting to signal that time is valuable.
Make a visible entrance with an opening statement as you walk in to establish your presence immediately.
Wait for the room to settle on its own before entering to avoid disrupting any conversations.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. Measured movement, personal acknowledgment, and patient stillness before speaking — that's the quiet authority of genuine executive presence.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either signals anxiety through haste, performs presence rather than embodying it, or misses the relationship-building opportunity of an entrance. Executive presence is earned in the stillness, not the noise. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to deliver your opening words once the room has settled — with full authority and calm.
response.success_feedback: That was commanding without being loud. You let the room come to you — and then you opened with intention. Real authority never needs to announce itself.

levels.title: Communicating Complex Strategy Simply
levels.scenario: You need to explain a multi-year strategic plan to an audience that includes both technical experts and non-technical board members.

mcq.question: What is the most effective approach for communicating a complex strategy to a mixed audience?
mcq.correct_option: Lead with the 'so what' — the strategic destination and why it matters — then layer in the how for those who need it, using plain language and a clear structure throughout.
incorrect_options: Present the full technical detail first so all audiences are working from the same comprehensive base.
Create two separate versions of the presentation — one for technical experts and one for board members.
Use strategic frameworks and business terminology since this is a senior audience that expects it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Start with the destination and the why, then layer the how — that structure works for every level of audience simultaneously.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either loses the room in detail, doubles the workload unnecessarily, or mistakes jargon for clarity. Great strategy communication is simple — by design. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to open your strategic plan presentation in a way that immediately connects with both the technical experts and the board members in the room.
response.success_feedback: Brilliantly clear! You started with meaning — not detail — and structured the message so it worked for every person in the room at once. That's strategic communication at the executive level.

levels.title: Presenting to the Board
levels.scenario: You are presenting a significant new investment recommendation to your board of directors. Two board members are known to be sceptical of this type of initiative.

mcq.question: What is the most effective approach to presenting to a board that includes known sceptics?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge the legitimate concerns of sceptics directly in your presentation — before they raise them — and address them with evidence, while remaining confident in your recommendation.
incorrect_options: Avoid mentioning known concerns to prevent giving them more weight than they deserve.
Have an ally on the board speak first to warm up the room before your presentation.
Present to the neutral board members and manage the sceptics in the Q&A rather than the presentation itself.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Pre-empting the sceptics' concerns shows you've thought rigorously and disarms their objections before they can interrupt your momentum.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either invites the concerns to surface uncontrolled, relies on political maneuvering, or splits your focus at the wrong moment. Address the sceptics' view before they raise it. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to present your investment recommendation to the board — including an effective pre-emption of the known sceptical view.
response.success_feedback: Outstanding! You faced the scepticism head-on within your own presentation, which is far stronger than waiting to be challenged. The board saw someone who had done the thinking. That's executive credibility.

levels.title: Inspiring Confidence in Uncertainty
levels.scenario: You are leading your organisation through a genuinely uncertain period. Stakeholders want reassurance, but you don't have certainty to offer.

mcq.question: How do leaders inspire confidence when they cannot offer certainty?
mcq.correct_option: Be honest about the uncertainty, demonstrate clarity of thinking about how you are navigating it, show what values and principles will guide your decisions, and commit to regular updates.
incorrect_options: Project maximum confidence to prevent stakeholders from becoming anxious or losing faith.
Focus communication on the parts of the future you can control and avoid mentioning uncertainties.
Provide detailed scenarios for each possible outcome so stakeholders feel fully informed.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right. Confidence in uncertainty doesn't come from projecting certainty — it comes from demonstrating clarity of thought, values, and process. That's what people really follow.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either misleads, creates selective transparency, or overwhelms with contingencies. Real confidence is in the navigation — not in false certainty. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to address your stakeholders in a way that is honest about uncertainty but genuinely inspiring in the face of it.
response.success_feedback: That was leadership of the highest order. You were honest, principled, and committed to your people — and you gave them something to follow that doesn't depend on knowing the future. That's real executive presence.

levels.title: Giving Feedback to a Senior Executive
levels.scenario: A senior executive on your leadership team has a communication style that is inadvertently shutting down junior voices in meetings. You are the only peer who has noticed and feels positioned to say something.

mcq.question: How do you give honest developmental feedback to a peer at the executive level?
mcq.correct_option: Request a private one-on-one, frame the conversation as coming from respect and care for the team, describe the specific behaviour and its impact with examples, and make the feedback an observation rather than a judgment.
incorrect_options: Raise it at a leadership team retrospective so the group can collectively address the team dynamic.
Mention it lightly in passing conversation without making it a full discussion to avoid making things awkward.
Tell the executive's line manager about the pattern and let them decide whether to address it.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Private, respect-framed, specific, observational — that's how you give feedback to a peer at seniority without it becoming political or personal.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either makes it public, too soft to land, or outsources a conversation that should come from you directly. Honest peer feedback is one of the most valuable gifts in leadership — give it directly and privately. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to give this senior executive peer honest and caring developmental feedback about their impact on the team.
response.success_feedback: That was real courage and real leadership. You gave specific, honest, caring feedback to someone at your level — in private — without making it about hierarchy or politics. That's how elite leadership teams get better.

levels.title: Shaping the Narrative
levels.scenario: Your organisation has made a controversial but necessary decision. Before the official announcement, internal speculation is building and the story is being shaped by rumour.

mcq.question: What is the most effective way to shape the narrative around a controversial decision?
mcq.correct_option: Get ahead of it — communicate the decision before rumour fully takes hold, explain the reasoning clearly and honestly, and frame the decision around the values and long-term interest it serves.
incorrect_options: Wait for the official announcement date and trust that the official communication will correct the speculation.
Deny any knowledge of the decision when asked directly to prevent premature information from spreading.
Communicate only the facts of the decision without the reasoning to avoid over-explaining or creating debate.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly! Getting ahead of the narrative with honesty, clear reasoning, and a values-based frame is how leaders shape — rather than react to — the story.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either cedes the narrative to rumour, damages credibility through dishonesty, or leaves people without the context they need to understand and accept the decision. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to get ahead of this controversial decision — framing it honestly, clearly, and around the values it serves.
response.success_feedback: Really powerful narrative leadership! You told the story before it was told for you — and you told it with honesty and purpose. That's how executives shape culture, not just communicate policy.

levels.title: Challenging Conventional Wisdom
levels.scenario: You are in a senior leadership forum where a long-held strategic assumption is being discussed as fact. You have strong evidence suggesting it may no longer be true.

mcq.question: How do you effectively challenge a deeply-held assumption in a senior leadership forum?
mcq.correct_option: Acknowledge why the assumption made sense historically, then present your evidence clearly and humbly, frame it as a question to explore rather than a position to win, and invite the group's scrutiny.
incorrect_options: Present your evidence confidently and state that the previous assumption was simply wrong.
Raise the question privately with the most influential person in the room before the forum, to gauge receptivity.
Wait until the broader strategy review to raise it so it has the right formal context.
mcq.correct_feedback: Exactly right! Historical respect, evidence presented humbly, framed as exploration — that's how you challenge conventional wisdom in a room full of people who helped create it.
mcq.incorrect_feedback: That approach either creates defensiveness, politicises it, or delays a conversation that needs to happen now. Challenge with evidence, respect, and genuine openness to being wrong yourself. Try again!

response.prompt: Choose 'Type' or 'Speak' to raise your evidence-based challenge to this long-held assumption in the senior leadership forum.
response.success_feedback: Brilliantly done! You challenged without attacking, presented evidence without arrogance, and invited the group into the question. That's how great strategies get updated — and great leaders earn lasting respect.

levels.title: Aligning Competing Stakeholders
levels.scenario: Three business units in your organisation each want different things from a shared resource that cannot fully serve all three simultaneously. You need to bring them to alignment.

mcq.question: What is the most effective approach to aligning stakeholders with competing interests?
mcq.correct_option: Bring all three parties together, establish the shared organisational goal first, and then work collaboratively to determine which allocation of the resource best serves that shared goal — with transparent trade-off conversations.
incorrect_options: Gather each party's position separately and then determine the fairest allocation independently.
Allocate the resource based on which unit has historically generated the most value for the organisation.
Escalate the decision to the CEO to avoid the political complexity of facilitating it yourself.

levels.title: Holding Your Values Under Pressure

mcq.question: What does holding your values under this kind of pressure actually look like?

Postpone the decision to buy time for the pressure to reduce before you have to make a stand.
